A bumper harvest at {place}: the barns are full and {good} is cheap as chaff. Buy now, sell in the lean weeks.
{place} cannot eat all its {good}: the criers call for buyers before it rots in the barns.
coronation: Hear ye! {ruler} is crowned in {kingdom}. Long may they reign!
By order of the crown of {kingdom}: {ruler} sits the throne, and all oaths are owed anew.
The bells of {kingdom} ring for {ruler}, crowned this week before the lords of the realm.
realm_fallen: Hear ye! The realm of {kingdom} is no more. Its banners are struck and its towns bow to new masters.
Mourn {kingdom}: its last walls have fallen and its crown is broken.
realm_restored: Hear ye! The banners of {kingdom} fly again over its old towns!
{kingdom} rises from its ashes. Let all who remember it rejoice.
peace: Hear ye! {kingdom} and {other} have made peace. Let the swords be sheathed and the roads reopen.
By treaty sealed: the war between {kingdom} and {other} is ended.
Peace between {kingdom} and {other}! The levies march home before the frost.
war: Hear ye! {kingdom} and {other} are at war. Every able man to his lord's banner!
War is declared between {kingdom} and {other}. Travellers, keep to the high roads.
saga_end: So ends {saga}. {title}. Let the tale be told in every hall.
revolt: Hear ye! {leader} and the lords with them rise against the crown of {kingdom}!
Rebellion in {kingdom}! {leader} raises banners against the throne.
revolt_end: Hear ye! The revolt in {kingdom} is ended. The realm is one again, for now.
The rebel banners in {kingdom} are lowered. The crown's peace returns.
rebellion: Hear ye! The common folk of {place} have risen against the lords of {kingdom}.
Unrest in {kingdom}: {place} is in open rebellion.
discovery: Hear ye! A new land is charted: {place}, found by {by}.
The map-makers add a new name: {place}, first sighted by {by}.
wonder: Hear ye! The {title} stands complete at {place}, raised by {by}!
A wonder for the ages: {by} has finished the {title} at {place}.
wonder_begun: Hear ye! {by} lays the first stone of the {title} at {place}.
Masons flock to {place}: {by} means to raise the {title}.
siege_won: Hear ye! {place} has fallen to {by} after {days} day(s) of siege.
{place} is taken! The siege laid by {by} is ended in victory.
siege_lost: Hear ye! The siege of {place} is broken. {by}'s host is driven off.
{place} holds! After {days} day(s), {by} gives up the siege.
lair_cleared: Hear ye! The outlaws of {place} are put down by {by}. {leader} will trouble the roads no more.
{place} is burned out! {by} has ended {leader} and the roads are safe again.
lair_risen: Beware! The outlaws of {place} under {leader} terrorise the country of {kingdom}. Travel in company.
A price is cried on {leader} of {place}, whose riders burn the villages of {kingdom}.
bank_failed: Hear ye! {bank} of {place} has shut its doors. Depositors are bidden to the receivers.
{bank} is broken! The strongrooms of {place} stand empty, and many a purse with them.
crown_default: Hear ye! The crown of {kingdom} will not pay its creditors. The bankers weep and the realm trembles.
By order of the crown, the debts of {kingdom} are repudiated. Let lenders beware.
coin_debased: Know all: the mint of {kingdom} strikes new coin of {purity} parts silver in the hundred. Prices rise in every market.
The coin of {kingdom} is clipped and thinned. Merchants weigh it twice and ask for more.
caravan_taken: Hear ye! The {good} {carrier} bound for {place} was taken by {by} on the road from {from}. Expect dear {good} in {place}.
Ill news on the roads: {by} fell on the {good} {carrier} of {house} between {from} and {place}.
The {good} {carrier} to {place} never came in. {by} have it, and the stalls of {place} stand empty.

true: A merchant back from {fashionPlace} swears {fashionText}: {fashionGoods} are fetching a premium wherever the fashion has reached.
The pedlars say {fashionGoods} sell for twice their worth since the court at {fashionPlace} took them up.
false: They say the court at {fashionPlace} is sick of {fashionGoods} already. Nobody wants them now.
A drunk swears the new fashion is wooden shoes. Nobody believes him, but nobody knows better.

true: Bread in {kingdom} is up {pricePct}% since {sinceSeason}, the gazette says. Grain carters are doing well.
The gazette nailed up at the market says prices in {kingdom} are {pricePct}% above {sinceSeason}'s.
false: Prices are falling in {kingdom}, they say. The gazette must be wrong.
Some say bread will be cheap again by the next market day. Some say a lot of things.

true: {kingdom} and {enemy} are at each other's throats. The levies left last week.
A soldier home on leave says the war with {enemy} is going hard for {kingdom}.
false: Word is {kingdom} and {enemy} have signed a truce already.
A drover swears the war with {enemy} is over. He sounded very sure.

true: {blockader}'s ships hold the harbour mouth. Nothing sails out of {settlement} without their leave.
The fishers say {blockader}'s galleys sit off the coast day and night.
false: The blockade? Lifted, they say. {blockader}'s ships sailed home.
Someone swears the harbour is open again. Nobody has seen it with their own eyes.

true: {siegeTown} is under siege. The camp-followers say the stores won't last.
Smoke over {siegeTown} again. The siege goes on.
false: They say {siegeTown} opened its gates yesterday.
A tinker swears the siege of {siegeTown} was lifted days ago.

true: Talk is all of the {eventName} at {eventPlace}.
A carter just in from {eventPlace} says the {eventName} is real enough.
false: Someone swears the {eventName} at {eventPlace} is over already.
They say the {eventName} at {eventPlace} was never as bad as the criers made out.

true: Everyone is talking about {saga}. Nobody sleeps easy.
A pilgrim brought news of {saga}: it isn't over.
false: {saga}? Old wives' tales. It ended months ago, they say.
A bard swears {saga} is finished. Bards say a lot of things.

true: {rival} passed through here not long ago. {rivalNews}
You've just missed {rival}. They drank here and left a story behind.
false: {rival} is dead, they say. Fell off a cliff, or was it a horse?
Someone saw {rival} heading the other way entirely.

true: {ruler} wears the crown of {kingdom} now. {oldRuler} is gone.
New coins already, with {ruler}'s face on them.
false: They say {oldRuler} isn't dead at all, only hiding.
A pedlar swears {ruler} won't last the season. Who knows.

true: Lords are in revolt across {kingdom}. Choose your roads carefully.
The rebels hold towns in {kingdom}. Taxes go to whoever has the most spears.
false: The revolt? Bought off already, they say.
I heard the rebels in {kingdom} all surrendered. I heard wrong before.

true: The crier was here: {proclamation}
Did you hear the herald? {proclamation}
false: The crier said something about a crown, or a war. I was drinking.
A herald came through, but folk can't agree on what he said.

lines: They've called up every second son in {settlement} for the war with {enemy}.
War with {enemy}. Bread costs more and nobody knows when it ends.
My cousin marched off against {enemy} in the spring. Not a letter since.
If {enemy} comes this far, I'm taking the cart and the goats to the hills.
Every night the watch doubles. That's what war with {enemy} looks like from here.
Eyes open, stranger. We're at war with {enemy}, and spies come in all shapes.
Half the garrison went to the front against {enemy}. The rest of us sleep in our boots.
Captain says {enemy} scouts were seen two days out. Keep your blade handy.
The war with {enemy} has closed half my roads. Prices go up, and I can't help it.
Iron and horses sell themselves while {kingdom} fights {enemy}. Grain too.
I lost a whole wagon to {enemy} raiders last month. War is ruin for honest trade.
The lord's men took two of my oxen for the war against {enemy}. Who'll plough now?
War with {enemy}, and still the fields want sowing. Nobody fights a war on an empty belly.
They burn the fields first, the soldiers. Pray {enemy} never comes up this valley.
I bury the sons this war with {enemy} sends home. Pray for peace, traveller.
The shrine fills with mothers lighting candles for their boys at the front.
The crown wants more men for the war with {enemy}, and more silver. Always more silver.
A war with {enemy} is a fine thing for a family with ambitions. Ruinous for one without.
Spearheads, spearheads, spearheads. The war with {enemy} eats iron faster than I can forge it.
I haven't made a plough blade in weeks. The war with {enemy} wants swords.
I'm charging the crown double, and they pay it. That tells you how the war with {enemy} goes.
Lost my leg the last time {kingdom} fought {enemy}. A copper for an old soldier?
War makes beggars faster than any plague. Spare something?
My da says {enemy} soldiers eat children. Is that true?
We play knights and {enemy}. I'm always the knight!
I came the long way round. The roads near {enemy}'s border are crawling with patrols.
Saw a column marching to the front against {enemy}. Boys, most of them.
If they'd give me a spear I'd go myself. {enemy} needs a lesson.
Let {enemy} come. {settlement} has stood through worse.
I keep my head down and my door barred. Wars are for other people.
Best not to say too much about the war. You never know who's listening.
{kingdom} is at war with you, and you walk in here bold as brass?
The crown has put a price on your banners. I never saw you, understand?
Your war with {kingdom} has made you a lot of enemies here. Not me, mind. I sell to anyone.
{blockader}'s ships sit off the harbour. Nothing comes in and nothing goes out.
With the port shut by {blockader}, salt fish costs as much as beef.
The fishing boats stay tied up. {blockader}'s galleys sink anything that tries.
The blockade's strangling us. The harbour master drinks from noon now.
My cargo has sat on the quay for weeks. {blockader}'s blockade will ruin me.
Whatever you want from over the sea, it's dear. Blame {blockader}.
Smugglers still slip past {blockader}'s ships at night, if you know who to ask. I don't, of course.
My man fished for a living. Now he sits by the fire and curses {blockader}.
When the harbour's shut, the poor eat last.
You can see the smoke from {siegeTown} on a clear day. The siege goes on.
Refugees from {siegeTown} sleep in the barns. They say the walls won't hold much longer.
They're starving {siegeTown} out. I pray it never comes to that here.
Every cart that leaves for {siegeTown} comes back empty and bloody.
If {siegeTown} falls, we're next. The captain's had us drilling at dawn.
We've orders to turn back anyone fleeing {siegeTown} without papers. Grim work.
Bread for the siege camp at {siegeTown} sells at three times the price. War is good for someone.
I won't send a wagon near {siegeTown}. Both sides steal from carts.
Cold enough to freeze the ale in the barrel. Keep near the fire, traveller.
The passes are snowed shut. Nobody travels in winter if they can help it.
Wolves come close to the walls in winter. Mind the roads at dusk.
Spring at last. The roads are mud, but at least they're open.
Lambing season. Half the town hasn't slept in a week.
Summer's when the lords go to war. Dry roads, full granaries.
Long days and short tempers. Summer in {settlement} is always the same.
Harvest time! Every hand is in the fields, mine included.
Grain is cheap now. By spring it'll cost you dear. Buy while you can.
The harvest fair is coming. Best time of year in {settlement}.
The barley is in, thank the gods. Now to get it to the mill before the rain.
Good harvest or bad, the lord takes his share first.
Sowing time. If you've strong arms, there's work in the fields for a few coppers.
Pray for gentle rain. A wet spring and a dry summer, that's what we want.
There's no work in {settlement}. Half the men on my street stand at the corner from dawn to dusk.
The masters aren't hiring. If you've a job going, there's a dozen strong backs here would take it.
Idle hands, they say. Well, there's a lot of idle hands in {settlement} these days, and purses going missing.
Refugees, all over the square. Poor souls came with what they could carry.
We've folk sleeping in the church porch. They fled the fighting, they say. Bread's gone dearer since.
More mouths, same bread. The newcomers will work for anything, and the old hands don't like it.
The guilds have downed tools. Not a hammer in {settlement} till the masters pay a wage that buys bread.
Strike's on. The workshops are cold and the journeymen are in the taverns, singing rude songs about the masters.
Work for anyone who wants it in {settlement}. The workshops are hiring and the newcomers keep coming.
Good times. My cousin came in from the village last month and found a place the same week.
They've struck a new vein up in the hills. Half the lads in {settlement} have gone up with a pick.
A new mine, they say. More hands wanted, more mouths to feed, more coin in the taverns.
The mine's worked out. The miners are packing their carts; the smiths will pay through the nose for ore now.
Nothing left in those hills but holes. My brother dug there twenty years; now he's off to find work elsewhere.
A day's wage doesn't buy a day's bread any more. Something's got to give.
We work, and we still go hungry. My father says it wasn't like this in his day.
There's no {dearthGood} to be had in {settlement}, not for love nor money. Well, money, if you've a lot of it.
The stalls ran out of {dearthGood} days ago. The carters say the roads are bad.
{dearthGood}? You'll pay twice what it's worth here, if you find any at all.
Bring {dearthGood} to {settlement} and name your price. We've none.
Whoever hauls {dearthGood} in here this week will go home rich.
Everyone's short of {dearthGood}. The rich buy it all and the rest of us go without.
{settlement} is drowning in {glutGood}. You could buy a cartload for a song.
Too much {glutGood} and nobody to sell it to. Prices have fallen through the floor.
The {strikeGuild} has shut its doors. No {strikeGood} till the crown listens, they say.
Have you heard? The {strikeGuild} is out. You'll pay through the nose for {strikeGood} this week.
My cousin's in the {strikeGuild}. They'd sooner starve than work for what the stalls pay now.
With the {strikeGuild} out, anyone who brings {strikeGood} to {settlement} names his price.
Strikebreaking's a dangerous trade, friend. The {strikeGuild} remembers faces.
{glutGood} is cheap as dirt here. Carry it where they're short and you'll do well.
I can't shift my {glutGood}. Take some off my hands, cheap.
These are the lean weeks. The granary's near empty and the new crop's a long way off.
Everyone tightens their belt this time of year. Some have no belt left to tighten.
Bread's dear and getting dearer. Spring can't come soon enough.
The lean season. Children cry at night here, and not from bad dreams.
Haven't eaten since yesterday. Anything, please. Anything at all.
The temple ran out of bread this morning. Have you a crust?
Food's the best trade in the lean weeks. Anyone who stored grain at harvest is rich now.
Sell me your grain and I'll pay you well. In the lean season everyone is hungry.
We're eating the seed corn now. That's how lean it is.
Old Hobb slaughtered his last pig to get through the lean weeks. Next year will be harder.
Plague at {eventPlace}. They've shut the gates there, and they burn the dead at night.
Keep your distance, stranger. They say the sickness at {eventPlace} spreads on the breath.
Vinegar on a cloth over your mouth. That's what the physicians say. For all the good it does.
Three carts of dead from {eventPlace} yesterday. I counted.
The plague at {eventPlace} is a judgement, some say. I say it is a sickness, and we must tend the sick.
I go to {eventPlace} tomorrow to give the last rites. Pray for me.
Herbs and remedies, very dear while the plague's at {eventPlace}. I won't apologise.
The granaries of {eventPlace} are bare. People are eating bark bread.
Hungry months. My neighbour sold his cow for a sack of oats.
If you have food to sell, sell it here. People are desperate.
Famine makes thieves of honest folk. Watch your packs.
Not a drop of rain in weeks. The wells around {eventPlace} are dry.
The river's so low you can walk across it. Bad for the mills, bad for the crops.
The priests pray for rain every morning. The sky ignores them.
The floods near {eventPlace} took whole villages. Mud up to the rooftops.
Don't take the low road. It's under water since the floods.
Bandits rule the roads near {eventPlace} now. Travel in company or not at all.
The bandit gang near {eventPlace} took a whole caravan. Killed the drivers.
The lord does nothing about the bandits. Maybe the lord is paid not to.
Pirates off {eventPlace}. No captain will sail without an escort.
Black sails near {eventPlace}. Three ships lost this month.
Gold near {eventPlace}! Half the young men left with picks and dreams.
My brother went prospecting at {eventPlace}. He came back with a cough and no gold.
The markets of {eventPlace} have crashed. Merchants hang themselves over their ledgers.
Nobody's buying. Nobody's selling. Coin's gone to ground since the crash.
Business is good! Caravans every day since trade picked up in {eventPlace}.
Never seen so many merchants on the roads. Good times, while they last.
Something big near {eventPlace}. Took three sheep and a shepherd.
They're offering silver for whoever kills the beast at {eventPlace}. No takers yet.
I heard it howling last night. Don't laugh, I heard it.
Did you see the comet? A sword of fire in the sky. Something terrible is coming, mark me.
The priests say the comet is an omen. They never say of what.
The sun went black at noon! I've never been so frightened in my life.
The ground shook near {eventPlace}. Walls fell, and the temple bell rang by itself.
Since the earthquake I sleep outside. Roofs fall, the sky doesn't.
A grand festival in {eventPlace}! Music and free ale, they say.
Everyone's off to the festival. I'm stuck minding the house.
Refugees pour into {eventPlace}. Poor souls, but where will they all sleep?
There's a new face on every corner since the refugees came. Some folk don't like it.
The blizzard buried the roads around {eventPlace}. Nobody's moving until the thaw.
Snow to the eaves. Two travellers froze on the road last night.
Best harvest in living memory around {eventPlace}! The granaries are bursting.
So much grain this year they're giving it to the pigs. Imagine!
The faithful are at each other's throats again. Schisms, crusades, I keep out of it.
The priests preach war from the pulpit now. That never ends well.
The lords are in revolt. Nobody knows who to pay taxes to any more.
Rebels hold the next town. If they come here, keep your mouth shut and your door barred.
Some say the rebels are right. I say nothing. Saying things gets you hanged.
A revolt is a dangerous game. Pick the winning side early, I always say.
My cousin rides with the rebels. I write to him every week, and to the crown every other week.
Nobody takes the road after dark now. Not with {leader}'s riders out of {lair}.
They hit a cart from {settlement} last week. Folk say it was the {lair} lot.
If the crown won't deal with {lair}, somebody should. There's a price on {leader}'s head, I hear.
My brother-in-law swears he saw smoke over {lair}. Bandits don't hide anymore, they build.
We'd clear out {lair} ourselves if the captain gave the word. He won't. Not enough of us.
Watch the roads, stranger. {leader} has eyes in every tavern from here to {lair}.
Lost two wagons on the road past {lair}. I pay guards now, and the guards cost more than the goods.
Go round {lair} if you value your purse. {leader} takes a toll in coin or in blood.
Bite the new coin and your teeth go through it. The crown's clipped it again.
Bread costs a third more than last year, and the baker swears it isn't his fault. It's the coin.
My grandmother's silver penny buys twice what the new ones do. I keep it under the floor.
I weigh every coin from {kingdom} twice now, and still lose on the exchange.
Prices in {settlement} are up, but so is everything I pay. Base coin makes fools of us all.
Another levy! The tax men took my second cow for the crown's war debts.
They say {ruler} owes the bankers more than the realm earns in a season. And who pays? We do.
The crown told the bankers it won't pay. Bold. Now nobody will lend to {kingdom} for a generation.
When kings don't pay their debts, why should anyone pay theirs? Mind you, the bailiffs still come for ours.
There's a crowd at the doors of {bank} since dawn, all waving their notes. I got out what I could.
They say {bank} can't pay out. If you've coin there, run, don't walk.
{bank} is broken. My savings with it. Thirty years at the loom, gone like smoke.
The receivers of {bank} pay a third of what's owed, they say, and take a year to do it.
My cousin put his savings in {listing}. Doubled in a month! I'm selling the mule to buy some.
Everyone's mad for {listing} at the Bourse. When the barber gives you tips on shares, sell.
{listing}'s shares aren't worth the paper now. My cousin's selling his mule back to me, at half.
They hanged a broker in effigy outside the Bourse. {listing} took half the town's savings with it.
The underwriters went bust. Every ship that sails from here now sails at its owner's risk.
{bank} won't pay the claims, they say. Insured! Ha. Insured against the insurers, that's what you'd need.
{bank} lends to kings and cobblers alike, at a price. Mind you pay it back. Their bailiffs don't knock twice.
Put your coin with {bank} if you've more than you can carry. Safer than under the bed, mostly.
Have you heard about {saga}? Everyone here talks of nothing else.
Strange times. {saga}, they're calling it. The old folk say it's like the stories.
My grandmother says {saga} is the end of the world. She said that about the last harvest too.
The wyrm! Burned a whole farmstead to ash near the peaks. You can see the scorch from the road.
The mountain shook and the wyrm came out. They say {villain}'s name in whispers.
Nobody grazes sheep on the high pastures any more. Not with the wyrm awake.
The Grey Cough. First you're tired, then you're coughing, then you're gone.
There's a scholar going about saying she can cure the Grey Cough. I hope she's right.
A lost heir, back from the dead? {villain}, he calls himself. Half the town believes him.
If the lost heir is real, there'll be war. If he's not, there'll be hangings.
This winter won't end. Frost in the fields well past when it should have thawed.
Bread riots in the next town over. The Long Winter, folk call it.
Black sails on the horizon. The reavers burned a fishing village not two days' sail from here.
{villain} leads the reavers, they say. A name to frighten children with.
There's a preacher splitting the faithful in two. Families won't sit at the same table.
Which side of the schism are you on? Careful how you answer here.
The Iron Company wasn't paid, so now they take what they're owed from us.
Sellswords with no master. {villain}'s men, they say. Lock up your daughters and your silver.
The comet grows redder every night. The prophets in the square say the end is near.
There's a cult now, worshipping the comet. Gave away all their goods. Fools.
{rival} was through here only days ago. Bought a round for the whole tavern.
You just missed {rival}! Same look in the eye as you, I'd say.
{rival} stayed a night and left before dawn. In a hurry to beat someone to something.
Everyone's talking about {rival}. You should do something worth talking about.
{rival} bought half my rope and all my torches. Off to some ruin, I suppose.
{rival} came through armed to the teeth. We watched that one closely. Same as you.
{rival} gave me a copper and showed me a real sword! Are you as famous as {rival}?
{oldRuler} is dead, and {ruler} wears the crown now. New ruler, new taxes, you'll see.
They rang the bells for {ruler} all day. I hope the new one is kinder than the old.
{ruler} on the throne. The coins with {oldRuler}'s face are still good, for now.
A new reign. Everyone's waiting to see which lords {ruler} favours.
The court is all a-flutter since {ruler} was crowned. Fortunes rise and fall in a day.
{ruler} hasn't yet named the new council. Every family in {kingdom} is scheming.
The crier was here: {proclamation}
A herald came through crying a coronation. A new crown, they say. Same old taxes.
Did you hear? {proclamation} I never thought I'd live to see it.
A whole realm gone. Kingdoms die like men, it seems.
Peace! The herald said so. {proclamation}
There's a treaty, the crier says. My boy might come home.
Peace, they say. I'll believe it when the soldiers are home and the taxes go down.
The crier was here yesterday. {proclamation}
War again, the herald says. It's always war again.
Did you hear the herald? {proclamation}
So that's over, then. The crier said as much. Folk will tell that tale for a hundred years.
The crier spoke of revolt. {proclamation}
A new land on the maps! {proclamation}
The herald says someone found an island no one knew. I'd like to see it, once.
Have you heard? {proclamation}
They say it can be seen from three days' ride. The crier tells it: {proclamation}
Stone and gold and a thousand masons. Folk will travel far to gape at it.
The herald brought news of a siege won. {proclamation}
Walls fall and banners change. The crier tells it like a song.
Did you hear the crier? {proclamation} Prices will climb, mark my words.
Embargoes, duties... the merchants grumble and the smugglers grin.
My cousin hauls salt over that border. Now he hauls it by night.
The herald says there's a trade treaty signed. {proclamation}
No more duties at the border, they say. The carters will be glad of it.
{proclamation} About time the crown thought of its own people.
Grain stays in the realm now, the crier says. The farmers near the border are furious.
Bad news from the crier: {proclamation}
A siege lost, the herald says. Somebody's sons won't come home.
You're the one who sacked {deedPlace}. I've heard the stories. Every one of them.
They say you burned {deedPlace} and took the coin from the temple. Is it true?
*steps back* Please, we've nothing worth taking here. Not like {deedPlace}.
You fed {deedPlace} through the hungry winter. People remember a thing like that.
The grain carts at {deedPlace} were yours, weren't they? Gods bless you for it.
My sister lives in {deedPlace}. She says your grain kept her children alive.
You pardoned that one at {deedPlace}. Mercy or weakness, folk can't agree.
A pardon at {deedPlace}! You've a soft heart, or a clever head.
You beat {deedVictim} in a duel near {deedPlace}! I'd have paid to see it.
They're saying you put {deedVictim} on their back. Was it a clean fight?
The duel near {deedPlace} is all anyone talks about. You've made a name, friend.
*goes pale* Y-yes, my lord. Whatever you need. Anything.
They say you hang men from the gate and leave them for the crows. I'll cause you no trouble.
Mothers frighten their children with your name. I didn't think you'd be so... ordinary-looking.
*bows low, trembling* We heard you were coming. The whole street went quiet.
Captain says to give you no cause for anger. Pass, my lord. Quickly.
I'll look the other way, my lord. I've a family.
*runs to hide behind a barrel*
Bless you, friend. Folk say you never pass a shrine without kneeling.
The gods favour you, they say. Would you say a prayer for my sick mother?
A pious soul in these hard times. You give me hope.
Your devotion is spoken of even in the high temple. Walk in the light, child.
Kneel with me a moment. It is rare to meet a lord who means the prayers.
You're the one who burns heretics, aren't you? I've always been very devout. Very.
Folk say you'd put a whole town to the torch for the faith. Is that holy?
I've heard what you do to people who cross you. I won't cross you.
*won't meet your eyes* Please, just tell me what you want.
You spared the beaten when you could have killed them. Not many lords would.
They say you've a kind heart. Kind hearts are rare these days.
You're the merciful one. My uncle owes you his life, he says.
They say you charge at the head of your men. The soldiers love you for it.
First into the fight, last out. That's what they sing about you.
*smirks* Not running away today, then?
The soldiers have a song about you. It's not a nice one.
An open hand, they say you have. The poor of {settlement} bless your name.
You bought the whole tavern a round last time. Folk haven't forgotten.
Counting coins again? They say you'd sell your mother for a good margin.
Hide the silver, here comes the miser. *laughs nervously* Only joking.
It's you! My children will never believe I spoke to you!
The whole town loves you, you know. We'd follow you anywhere.
Kinslayer. *spits* The gods will have their due from you.
Your own blood. How do you sleep at night?
The champion of the lists! I won a silver on you at the last tourney.
Will you be riding in the next tournament? The whole town would come.
Tavern's that way, if you're looking. You usually are, they say.
*sniffs* Started early today?
A sea wolf, they call you. The salt's in your blood, I can tell.
They say you've read every book in three kingdoms. Can you read this letter for me?
The merchant prince himself! Half the caravans on these roads carry your goods.
They say you could buy {settlement} twice over. Could you?
Your word's good as gold, folk say. Rare in a lord.
Silver-tongued, they call you. I'll count my change twice, if it's all the same.
Back on the road again? You've seen more of the world than anyone in {settlement}.
They say you're always three moves ahead. I'll keep my secrets to myself, then.
Fancy a game of dice? No? They say you never refuse.
That scar... I've heard the story. Was it really a bear?
They say you judge with mercy. My brother's in a debtors' cell. Would you hear his case?
A merciful lord. Folk go to your court hoping, not trembling.
Your court hangs thieves by the dozen, they say. I've never stolen a thing in my life.
Hard justice at your court, folk say. Hard, but the roads are safer.
The gallows at your seat are never empty, I hear.
A fair judge, they call you. The poor get a hearing at your court as well as the rich.
If I've a quarrel with my neighbour, I'd want you to hear it.
Your court favours the temples, they say. The priests sing your praises.
A lord who listens to the clergy. My mother would approve.
Your court opens its purse to petitioners, they say. Is it true?
Folk say you never send a hungry man away from your hall.
*drops to one knee* Your Majesty! In {settlement}! Nobody told us!
Long live the crown! Forgive me, Majesty, I didn't recognise you at first.
Your Majesty. The taxes are heavy, if I may say so. Only if I may.
The king, here, in the street! Wait till I tell my wife.
Majesty. My family has always been loyal, whatever you may have heard.
*snaps to attention* Your Majesty! The watch is at your command!
A foreign crown, walking our streets. The lords here will want to know why.
You're a king, they say. Not ours, though. Mind that.
You're the one pressing a claim to the throne! Bold. Maybe mad.
Folk are choosing sides in your war for the crown. I choose to keep my head.
If you win, remember {settlement} was kind to you. If you lose, we never met.
An exile, they say. A crown lost. That's a hard road.
You had a throne in your grasp once. Now look at you.
Exiles come through here sometimes. Most never go home.
{house}! My father spoke of your father. Or was it your grandfather?
An old name, {house}. Folk here remember it.
The {house} line goes on, I see. Good. The world needs old families.
{house} has been in the songs for generations. And here's another of you!
Three generations of {house}, and the name only grows.
{house} is the talk of every hall. Mind the envy that comes with that.
Every noble family wants a marriage with {house} these days. So my mistress says.
There's something cold about you. The dogs won't stop barking.
Folk cross the street when you pass. I'd guess you know why.
Are you really {player}? The {player}? Can I touch your sword?
Your name's known three kingdoms over, {player}. I heard it in a tavern by the sea.
Bread is dear in {kingdom}: up {pricePct}% since {sinceSeason}. My children eat porridge twice a day now.
A loaf costs what a pie did in {sinceSeason}. {pricePct}% more, the baker says, and he's not lying.
Food's {pricePct}% dearer than in {sinceSeason}. Bring grain to {kingdom} and you'll sell it before you unload.
Grain's fetching {pricePct}% more than in {sinceSeason}. A cart from a glutted town would pay for itself twice.
I've never seen bread so dear in {kingdom}. Whoever's sitting on a granary is a rich man this season.
Everything costs {pricePct}% more than in {sinceSeason}. My wages don't.
Prices in {kingdom} are up {pricePct}% since {sinceSeason}. Buy today, for tomorrow it costs more.
{pricePct}% dearer than in {sinceSeason}, and they tell us the coin is sound.
Bread's cheap in {kingdom} this season. The farmers grumble, everyone else eats.
Food has never been so cheap. A good year, or a glut: depends whether you grow it or eat it.
Have you seen the fields? Half the ears are empty. It'll be a thin harvest this year, mark me.
No rain when we wanted it, rain when we didn't. The crop is poor; buy your flour now, while it's cheap.
The reeve walked the fields and came back grey. Bread will be dear by spring.
Never seen the wheat stand so tall. There'll be grain to spare this autumn, and cheap.
A fat year coming. The farmers say the barns won't hold it all.
Rust in the wheat, red as a fox. The whole valley's got it.
They're burning the blighted fields out past the mill. The smoke's been up for days.
Locusts! A cloud of them came over the ridge and ate the barley to the ground.
You can hear them at night, chewing. By morning there's nothing green left.
Murrain among the cattle. The herdsmen are burning carcasses on the common.
Half my neighbour's sheep dead in a week. Meat will be dear, and wool.
A poor harvest, and the winter not yet begun. Folk are counting every loaf.
The granary's half empty already. Pray the spring comes early.
A rich harvest this year. Bread's cheap and the ale's flowing.
Barns full to the rafters. The farmers complain grain fetches nothing, but nobody goes hungry.
Have you heard? At {fashionPlace}, {fashionText}. Every lady wants {fashionGoods} now.
So they say at {fashionPlace}: {fashionText}. The merchants can't get {fashionGoods} fast enough.
The fashion from {fashionPlace} is for {fashionGoods}. Sell them here and name your price.
One must have {fashionGoods} this season. At {fashionPlace} {fashionText}, and I will not be thought provincial.
Everyone at {fashionPlace} wants {fashionGoods}. I paid twice their worth and was glad of it.
If you deal in {fashionGoods}, the courts will pay a premium until the fashion passes. It always passes.

patronage._comment: Patronage & Great Works (src/systems/patronage.js). Clients (artists, scholars, architects, physicians, chroniclers) are offered in a town's salon, chosen by a hash of the world seed, the town and the month (no RNG). They draw a weekly stipend, produce works on commission and can be poached by rival Houses or leave when unpaid or idle. Great Works are multi-stage projects at a settlement the player rules or holds a house in: each stage wants goods + gold delivered, then days of paid labour. Every effect key has a reader: research (Technology.getResearchBonus), conversion (PlayerReligion.conversionMultiplier), education (Upbringing growth), vision (Player.updateVisibility), festivalRenown (Festivals.getReputation), riverCross (Infrastructure.getRiverPenalty), care/woundHeal (Ailments), mood (Taxation happiness target via settlement.patronage), monthlyPrestige (House Prestige, paid by Patronage). Kingdoms build wonders too (npc*), first to finish a unique work claims it for the world.
